questions.qtext: What is the smallest positive integer $n$ such that there is a group of order $n$ which is not abelian?
questions.solution:
Answer: 6

Source solution 1 (score: 18)

Okay let proceed with the answer, please note the following points:

  1. There is only one non isomorphic group of order 1 i.e ({e}, *) and this is Cyclic.
    * e
    e e
  2. For a prime number p, every group of order p is cyclic. So group with order 2, 3, 5 are cyclic.
  3. For Order 4, only 2 non isomorphic groups are there which are:

    Template 1:
    * e a b c
    e e a b c
    a a e c b
    b b c e a
    c c b a e

    Template 2:
    * e a b c
    e e a b c
    a a e c b
    b b c a e
    c c b e a

    As you can see both are Abelian.

    OR
  4. Groups of order $p^{2}$, where p is prime, are necessarily Abelian. That rules out 4 as possible order of non-Abelian groups.
  5. There are two groups of order 6. One of these is cyclic. The other is the symmetric group on 3 symbols, S3. This group is non-Abelian.

    Example:
    Element 123 213 132 321 231 312
    123 123 213 132 321 231 312
    213 213 123 231 312 132 321
    132 132 312 123 231 321 213
    321 321 231 312 123 213 132
    231 231 321 213 132 312 123
    312 312 132 321 213 123 231

    Reference: https://groupprops.subwiki.org/wiki/Symmetric_group:S3

    So, Answer is 6.

Some Important Points about Abelian Groups: https://www.youtube.com/live/Zb4OWjHL3yU?t=2180&feature=shared

The smallest non-abelian group has order $6.$

$\textbf{(Lagrange’s theorem) :}$ Let $\text{G}$ be a finite group and $\text{H} \subset \text{G}$ a subgroup of $\text{G}.$ Then $|\text{H}|$ divides $|\text{G}|.$

We know that If $\text{G}$ is a finite group with $|\text{G}|$ prime, then $\text{G}$ is cyclic.

$\textbf{Proof :}$ Let $p = |\text{G}|.$ Since $p \geq 2,$ there is an element $g \in \text{G}$ with $g \neq e.$ Consider the subgroup $\langle g \rangle \subset G$ generated by $g.$ We have $| \langle g \rangle | \geq 2$ since both $e, g \in \langle g \rangle.$ So by Lagrange’s theorem $| \langle g \rangle | = p.$ Thus $\langle g \rangle = \text{G},$ and so, by definition, $\text{G}$ is cyclic as claimed.

Every cyclic group is abelian.

$\text{Classification of Groups of Order}\; n \leq 5 :$

  • $n=1:$ The trivial group $\langle e \rangle$ is the only group with $1$ element.
  • $n=2,3,5 :$ These orders are prime, so Lagrange implies that any such group is cyclic.
  • $n=4 :$ There are only two groups of order $4,$ both are abelian.

questions.qtext: Let $\mathbf{Z}$ be the group of all integers under the operation of addition. Which of the following subsets of $\mathbf{Z}$ is/are NOT a subgroup of $\mathbf{Z}?$
questions.solution:
Answer: B

Source solution 1 (score: 16)

Since the operation is addition and addition is associative and a binary operation and its closed, Z under addition is a semigroup

For monoid, it must satisfy the properties of a semigroup and an unique identity must exist. For Z under addition, 0 is the identity element and $\forall x \epsilon Z, x + 0 = x$ and hence Z under addition is a monoid

A Group must satisfy the properties of a semigroup , monoid and in addition to that has an inverse element and also its closed under all operations

Given a group G, subset H of G is a subgroup of G if H also forms a group under the same operation

Order of the group is number of elements in the group (or) its cardinality

Also, by Lagrange’s theorem, order of the subgroup divides the order of the group

  1. Has only one element 0.

For addition operation, 0 is the identity and 0 + inverse(0) = identity $\Rightarrow$ 0 + 0 = 0. As we can see this subset is a subgroup as it satisfies properties of a group and also its closed

  1. Identity element 0 is not part of the subset. Inverse for each element is also not part of the subset. Since this subset is not closed , this is not a subgroup
  2. 0 is an even integer and part of the subset. For every even integer say x, -x is the inverse and -x is also part of the subset. Since this subset is closed , identity & inverse exists, this is a subgroup
  3. n is divisible by 6 and 9 $\Rightarrow$ n is divisible by LCM(6,9) which is 18. So, this subset contains multiples of 18 such as …, -54, -36, -18, 0, 18, 36, ….
    Identity element is 0 which is part of the subset
    Inverse of each element x is -x which is also unique and part of the subset.
    Hence, this subset is a subgroup

    Hence, correct option is B

questions.qtext: Which of the following multiplication tables defined on the set $G = \{a, b, c, d\}$ form a group?
questions.solution:
Answer: B, C

Source solution 1 (score: 8)

Option A table doesn’t have any identity element. There is no row exactly identical to the header. So, It’s not a group since it doesn’t have an identity. The easy way to see that it does not have an identity is that no row of the Cayley table matches the top row.

Option C table forms a group. It is the standard template where we have an identity element, one element who is inverse of itself, and two elements who are inverse of each other. So, it is a cyclic group.
The identity is a. All elements have inverses (the inverse of a is a, the inverse of b is b, the inverse of c is c and the inverse of d is d).


Option B table forms a group. It is the standard template where we have an identity element, and every element is inverse of itself. So, it is a group But not cyclic. The identity is a. All elements have inverses (the inverse of a is a, the inverse of b is b, the inverse of c is c and the inverse of d is d).


Option D is Not a group because, in the last row, element “d” repeats.
The identity is a. However, d does not have an inverse, so it is not a group.

Also, we know that every group of orders $4$ is abelian, hence we can eliminate options D, and A, as those are not commutative.


Analysis of Option C:

Source solution 2 (score: 4)

Ans is Option B and C.

An easy approach in these type of questions:-

First check which row is exactly same as the header row (a,b,c,d). The corresponding element in the operation column is the identity element.

Here, in option A, there is no such row. Hence no identity element. Hence option A is wrong.

Now in options B,C,D there is such a row, and all of them have the identity element as $’a’$. Now identity element must be in every row. But its absent in option D. So option D is wrong.

Now if we check in option B and C, we can see that they satisfy all the conditions. And every element has their own inverses. Inverses can be found by intersecting the corresponding row element and column element where the identity element (here $a$) is present.

Eg: In Option B → Inverse of a is a, b is b, c is c and d is d.

And in Option C → Inverse of a is a, b is d, c is c and d is b.

Let $\mathbf{Z}$ be set of integers, and “$+$” be an integer addition operation.

Let $p, q$ be distinct primes. If $\text{J}$ is a proper subgroup of $(\mathbf{Z}, +)$ containing exactly three of $\{p, p + q, pq, p^q, q^p\},$

(Note $:\text{J}$ may contain other elements of $\mathbf{Z}$ which are not in this set), which three elements does $\text{J}$ include?
questions.solution:
Answer: C

Selected solution (score: 30)

If element $\text{X}$ belongs to a group then $\text{X}^{n}$ should also belong to the group due to closure property and here

$\text{X}^{n} = \text{X + X + X } +\dots + \text{X} = (n\; \text{times X})$

The three elements are $p, pq$, and $p^q$ - these are the ones that can be obtained by repeatedly adding $p$ to itself.

Example : Let $\text{P} = 3 ; \text{Q} = 5$

Since $\text{J}$ is a proper subgroup of $(\mathbf{Z},+),$ So, J contains identity element i.e. $0;$

If $\text{J}$ contains $\text{P} = 3;$ then $\text{J}$ also has to contain $\text{P + P = 2P} = 6 ;$

  • $\text{P + P + P = 3P} = 9 ;$
  • $\text{P + P + P + P + P = 5P = PQ} = 15$
  • $\text{P + P} +\dots + (\text{P}^{\text{Q-1}}\;\text{times)} = \text{P}^{\text{Q}},$ etc.

$\textbf{NOTE:}$ If $\text{J}$ contains both $\text{P, Q}$ then $\text{J}$ would also contain $\text{P+Q} ; \text{P}^{\text{Q}} ; \text{Q}^{\text{P}} ; \text{PQ}$ etc..

BUT Since it is given that Exactly $3$ elements from $\{p, p + q, pq, p^{q}, q^{p}\};$ Option C is correct.

$\textbf{NOTE:}$ Since $\text{J}$ is proper subgroup of $(\mathbf{Z},+)$ hence, either $\text{J}$ is infinite set OR $\text{J} = \{0\}.$

  • Question: Proper subgroup $J$ containing exactly three of $\{p, p+q, pq, p^q, q^p\}$.

    • If $J$ contains $p$, it must contain all multiples of $p$, including $pq$ and $p^q$.

    • It cannot contain $p+q$ because if it contained $p$ and $p+q$, it would have to contain $(p+q) - p = q$. If it contains both primes $p$ and $q$, the subgroup is $1Z$ (all integers), which is not a proper subgroup.

  • Logic: * Subgroups of $(Z, +)$ are of the form $nZ$ (multiples of $n$).

  • Correct Answer: C ($\{p, pq, p^q\}$)

Let $\text{S}$ be the set of all functions $f : \text{R} \rightarrow \text{R}.$ Consider the two binary operations $+$ and $\ast$ on $\text{S}$ defined as pointwise addition and composition of functions, as follows.

  • $(f + g)(x) = f (x) + g(x)$
  • $(f \ast g)(x) = f (g(x))$

Which of the following statements are true?

  1. $\ast$ is commutative.
  2. $+$ and $\ast$ satisfy the left distributive law i.e. $f \ast (g + h) = (f \ast g) + (f \ast h).$
  3. $+$ and $\ast$ satisfy the right distributive law i.e. $(g + h)\ast f = (g \ast f)+ (h \ast f).$
questions.solution:
Answer: C

Source solution 1 (score: 20)
  • (f+g)(x) = f(x) + g(x) ..... (i)
  • (f*g)(x) = f(g(x)) ..... (ii)
1] * is commutative. i.e. we need to prove that, (f*g)(x) = (g*f)(x)
Proof: L.H.S. = (f*g)(x) = f(g(x)) ; 
 R.H.S. = (g*f)(x) = g(f(x)) _using (ii)
 ∴ 1] is FALSE since L.H.S. ≠ R.H.S. 
2] f * (g+h) = (f*g) + (f*h) ; i.e. [f * (g+h)](x) = (f*g)(x) + (f*h)(x)
Proof: L.H.S. = [f*(g+h)](x) = f((g+h)(x)) _using (ii) = f(g(x)+h(x)) _using (i) ; 
 R.H.S. = (f*g)(x) + (f*h)(x) = f(g(x)) + f(h(x)) _using (ii)
 ∴ 2] is FALSE since L.H.S. ≠ R.H.S.
3] (g+h) * f = (g*f) + (h*f) ; i.e. [(g+h) * f](x) = (g*f)(x) + (h*f)(x)
Proof: L.H.S. = [(g+h) * f](x) = (g+h)(f(x)) _using (ii) = g(f(x)) + h(f(x)) _using (i); 
 R.H.S. = (g*f)(x) + (h*f)(x) = g(f(x)) + h(f(x)) _using (ii)
 ∴ 3] is TRUE since L.H.S. = R.H.S.
Source solution 2 (score: 19)

Answer: C

I) $*$ is commutative:

Function composition is associative but not commutative.

Take for example $f(x) = x^2$ and $g(x) = x + 2$.

LHS: $fog(x) = f(g(x)) = f(x + 2) = (x + 2)^2$, whereas,

RHS: $gof(x) = g(x^2) = x^2 + 2$.

$fog(x) \neq gof(x)$.

II) $+$ and $∗$ satisfy the left distributive law i.e. $f∗(g+h)=(f∗g)+(f∗h)$.

Similar to above proof take some function $h(x) = x/2$.

LHS: $f * (g + h) = f[g(x) + h(x)] = f(x + 2 + x/2) = (x + 2 + x/2)^2$, whereas,

RHS: $(f ∗ g) + (f ∗ h) = f(g(x)) + f(h(x)) = f(x + 2) + f(x/2) = (x + 2)^2 + (x/2)^2$.

$f * (g + h) \neq (f * g) + (f * h)$.

III) $+$ and $∗$ satisfy the right distributive law i.e. $(g + h) ∗ f = (g ∗ f) + (h ∗ f)$.

LHS: $(g + h) ∗ f = (g + h)(f(x)) = (g + h)(x^2) = x^2 + 2 + x^2/2$.

RHS: $(g ∗ f) + (h ∗ f) = g(f(x)) + h(f(x)) = g(x^2) + h(x^2) = x^2 + 2 + x^2/2$.

So $(g + h) ∗ f = (g ∗ f) + (h ∗ f)$
